question: Does the measure behave the way the theory says it should?

cronbach1955.cite: Cronbach & Meehl (1955). Construct validity in psychological tests. Psychological Bulletin 52: 281–302.
cronbach1955.checked: every quote read word for word on 20 Nov 2026 in the full text at Classics in the History of Psychology (psychclassics.yorku.ca/Cronbach/construct.htm), which marks the journal's page breaks; page numbers are those marks; reference numbers are left out of the quotes

steps.title: Write the laws
steps.text: Spell out the theory around the construct as a set of linked claims: what it causes, what causes it, what it goes with.

quotes.text: Scientifically speaking, to "make clear what something is " means to set forth the laws in which it occurs. We shall refer to the interlocking system of laws which constitute a theory as a nomological network .

steps.title: Predict what tracks
steps.text: From the network, say in advance which other measures yours should correlate with, and which it should not.

quotes.text: If two tests are presumed to measure the same construct, a correlation between them is predicted.

steps.title: Predict who differs
steps.text: Say which groups should score differently, and in which direction, before you look.

quotes.text: If our understanding of a construct leads us to expect two groups to differ on the test, this expectation may be tested directly.

steps.title: Test the pattern
steps.text: Collect the data and check the whole set of predictions at once. Many varied hits count for more than a few similar ones.

quotes.text: Numerous successful predictions dealing with phenotypically diverse "criteria" give greater weight to the claim of construct validity than do fewer predictions, or predictions involving very similar behaviors.

steps.title: Read the misses
steps.text: A failed prediction does not say where the fault lies: the measure, the theory or the other measures. Find out which.

quotes.text: If the prediction is not confirmed, any link in the chain may be wrong.
